title: Why do literary agents keep rejecting my query letter? Fixes for Mac writers in 2026
metaTitle: Why do literary agents keep rejecting my query letter? (2026)
description: Agents reject most queries for a few common reasons: weak writing, a flat plot pitch, wrong genre, or a dull opening. Here is how to find yours on a Mac.
targetKeyword: why do literary agents keep rejecting my query letter

intro: Agents usually reject a query letter for a few repeat reasons: weak writing, a flat plot pitch, the wrong genre, a dull opening, an odd tone, and missed formatting rules. Agents seldom say which one applies to you. Test your letter against each reason, fix the likeliest one, and send a small batch again.
tldr: Agents rarely say why they pass. Most rejections point back to a short list of repeat problems.
The top reasons agents cite are weak writing, a plot pitch with no stakes, the wrong genre, and a boring opening.
A query letter should run one page or less, about 300 to 400 words.
Test your letter against each reason, change one thing at a time, and log every send.
Paid critiques cost about $50 to $175. The free fixes on this page come first.

blocks.text: Agents keep rejecting query letters for a short list of repeat reasons. Weak writing, a flat plot pitch, the wrong genre, a dull opening, a bad length, an odd tone, and missed formatting rules show up again and again. Agents seldom say which one applies to you. This page shows how to test your own letter against that list, one reason at a time, with fixes you can make on a Mac.
What the rejection numbers really show

Public data on query rejections is thin. I could not find a peer-reviewed study of rejection rates or reasons. The best figures come from QueryTracker averages, quoted secondhand by Rejectomancy, a writing blog. That post says the average querying author sends 44 queries. It reports an 87.8% rejection or closed-no-response rate and a 5.9% request rate.

Averages hide the detail. One author's postmortem from 2024 shows the spread more clearly. That writer sent 53 queries. The result was 35 rejections, 18 closed with no response, and 3 requests for the full manuscript. The author credited the premise as the biggest factor in the full requests. One author is not a sample, so treat this as a single case.

blocks.title: Read the rate correctly
blocks.text: A rejection rate of 87.8% does not mean your letter is broken. The figure counts silence as a no. Use these numbers to set expectations, then spend your effort on the part you control.
Why agents rarely tell you what went wrong

Rachelle Gardner, who writes about query rejections, says agents usually do not have time to explain why they pass. So rejections are mostly polite and generic. Phrases such as 'Not quite right for us' are euphemisms for no. You get very little feedback, so you have to diagnose the problem yourself.

Alyssa Matesic lists five reasons agents reject queries. They are an unprofessional letter, a lack of interest in the genre or current wants, an underwhelming plot blurb, a rough manuscript, and uninteresting sample pages. She calls sample pages the most common reason. She cites no statistics, only her experience reviewing hundreds of queries.

blocks.title: Look for clues in personal lines
blocks.text: A form rejection with one personal line is worth more than a blank pass. Gardner says personalized wording can point at the real problem. Save each reply in one folder, labeled with the agent name and date, so you can compare them later.
The reasons agents give most often

QueryTracker asked 144 agents for their top rejection reasons. The page ranks the answers but gives no vote counts or percentages. Read the order as a guide to where agents look first. It does not tell you how often each reason applies to any one letter.

rows: Read the letter out loud, one paragraph at a time
Events listed with no want, obstacle, or cost
Write one sentence each for want, obstacle, and cost
The agent's list does not match your book
Check the agent's own site and wish list
The letter runs past one page
Count words and aim for about 300 to 400
The pitch starts with setup, not trouble
Start with the main character facing a problem
Missing title, genre, or rounded word count
Compare against the agent's posted rules

blocks.text: Worked example: fixing a flat pitch

Here is a common flat pitch. Mara finds a letter in her late father's desk and begins to wonder about her family's past. The sentence is clear. It has no want, no obstacle, and no cost. An agent reads it and feels nothing about what happens next. This example is invented for illustration.

Now the revision. When Mara finds a letter saying her father is alive, she has until the funeral to learn why he hid it. If she fails, she loses the family farm. The rewrite names a deadline, a conflict, and a stake. Each part gives the agent a reason to keep reading.

Test the rewrite on someone who has not read your book. Ask them what Mara wants. If they hesitate, the pitch still misses its job. Rewrite until the answer comes fast. Then check that the pitch matches the first pages, because the agent will compare them.
Length, layout, and the sample pages

QueryTracker says a query letter should be one page or less, about 300 to 400 words. It should include the title, a rounded word count, the genre, and a short back-cover pitch. Credits, a reason for choosing the agent, and comps are optional. Long letters waste the agent's time, and length is on the top reasons list.

blocks.title: Sample pages can sink a good letter
blocks.text: A strong letter can still get a pass if the first pages slow down. Matesic calls sample pages the most common reason she sees. Before you send, check that the first page keeps the same energy the pitch promises.

items: Title and genre at the top, then the rounded word count
Agent name spelled right, with the salutation the agent prefers
Pitch in plain text in the email body, unless the agent asks for an attachment
Only the files the agent requests, in the format it asks for
One personal line that names something specific about the agent
No decorative fonts or bullet points that email may strip out

blocks.text: In Pages, every document begins with a template that you can replace with your own content, according to Apple. Pick a plain layout for the letter, so the formatting does not fight your email. Copy the final text into a mail draft and read it once more in the message window.
Mistakes people make when they fix a query

items: Changing the pitch, the opening, and the comps in one day, so you cannot tell what helped
Sending the same letter to every agent before you check each agent's fit
Treating one form rejection as proof the whole book fails
Replying to a rejection to argue or ask why, which Gardner advises against
Rewriting the whole novel when the letter is the actual problem
Querying before the manuscript is finished, when Quick Fox says the novel must be complete first

blocks.text: Query Shark takes a different route. It says there are no rejections. Queries are posted only when the writer asks, and queries that do not follow its posted directions are discarded. A query not posted within about 120 days probably will not be posted. Read that blog's rules before you send anything.
Where Lazur helps with query letter work

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur sees your screen, points at things, and answers out loud. It helps you ask about the page in front of you, such as which sentence is vague. It does not judge your book, and it does not send your email.

Hold fn to dictate. Dictation types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Speaking a revised pitch often exposes clumsy phrasing that you skip when you type. Dictation is unlimited on the Pro and Power plans, so you can revise by voice without using AI actions.
What a query problem costs you

Paid help has a clear price. Quick Fox Editors charges $50 per round of query critique, per item, with a 48-hour turnaround. Club Ed Freelancers charges $175 for a critique of a query up to 500 words. Both prices come from their own pages, and both can change.

Time has a cost too, but I found no data on how long agents take to respond. The Rejectomancy author who sent 53 queries logged 18 with no response. Waiting, and getting silence, is part of the cost. Plan for it so one slow agent does not stall the whole list.

Money matters here because book income is thin for many writers. The Authors Guild's 2023 survey reports a $10,000 median book income for full-time authors in 2022. For all authors, including part-time, the median was $2,000. At those numbers, a paid critique is a real decision.

blocks.title: A critique is not a guarantee
blocks.text: None of the critique pages I opened shows that a critique raises request rates. Pay only for a specific read you need, and try the free fixes first.
How to test a fix without guessing

Change one thing per batch, then track the results. Log each send in a Pages table or a spreadsheet, with the date, the version, the agent, and the reply. Two columns matter most: whether the agent asked for pages, and whether the reply was a pass or silence.

QueryTracker is a website, so it is not a Mac app. I did not find a Mac-native query tracker in my research. A plain table in Pages or Word does the job. The Pages templates give you a start on layout if you want one.
Start with one fix this week

Pick the single reason that fits your letter best. Fix it first, then send a small batch and wait. If replies stay the same, move to the next reason on the list. Keep each version of the letter as a separate file, so you can compare them later.

faq.question: Why do literary agents keep rejecting my query letter if my writing is good?
faq.answer: Good prose can still fail if the pitch lacks stakes, the genre fit is wrong, or the first pages drag. QueryTracker lists poor writing quality first, but many reasons sit outside sentence quality. Test the letter against each reason before you assume the book is the problem.

faq.question: Do literary agents explain why they reject queries?
faq.answer: Usually not. Rachelle Gardner says agents rarely have time to explain. Phrases such as 'Not quite right for us' usually mean no. Personalized wording can be a clue to the real problem, so save each reply.

faq.question: How long should a query letter be?
faq.answer: QueryTracker says one page or less, about 300 to 400 words. The letter should include the title, a rounded word count, the genre, and a short pitch. Credits, a reason for choosing the agent, and comps are optional.

faq.question: Is a paid query critique worth the money?
faq.answer: That depends on your budget. Quick Fox Editors charges $50 per round per item with a 48-hour turnaround. Club Ed Freelancers charges $175 for a letter up to 500 words. I found no study showing a critique raises request rates, so start with the free fixes.

faq.question: Should I respond to a rejection from an agent?
faq.answer: Rachelle Gardner advises writers not to respond to rejections. Log the reply, follow the agent's posted rules for any follow-up, and move to the next agent on your list.

faq.question: Can Lazur write my query letter for me?
faq.answer: Lazur drafts and types text, and it answers questions about what is on your screen. It does not send your email or click buttons in other apps. You decide what goes into the letter and what you send.

faq.question: Does QueryTracker have a Mac app?
faq.answer: No. QueryTracker is web-based, so it is not a Mac app. I did not find a Mac-native query tracker in my research, so a Pages table or a spreadsheet works for logging sends.

costs.title: Money for a paid critique
costs.text: Paid help has a clear price. Quick Fox Editors charges $50 per round of query critique, per item, with a 48-hour turnaround. Club Ed Freelancers charges $175 for a letter up to 500 words. Both prices come from their own pages, and both can change.

costs.text: I found no data on how long agents take to respond. The Rejectomancy author who sent 53 queries logged 18 closed with no response. Waiting, and getting silence, is part of the cost. Plan for it so one slow agent does not stall the whole list.

costs.title: Thin income behind the stakes
costs.text: The Authors Guild's 2023 survey reports a $10,000 median book income for full-time authors in 2022. For all authors, including part-time, the median was $2,000. At those numbers, a paid critique is a real decision, so weigh it against the free fixes.

costs.title: Emotional cost (not measured)
costs.text: I found no data on burnout, grades, or how long a rejection takes to recover from. This page does not put a number on them. Set your own limit, such as how many sends you can handle in a week, before you start.

causes.title: Weak writing in the letter
causes.text: QueryTracker's agent survey ranks poor writing quality first. Agents read the letter as a sample of your prose. Typos, tangled sentences, or vague verbs signal that the manuscript may need more work. You may not see the problem because you know the story. Read the letter cold, the next morning, and notice where you skip ahead. Those spots usually hold the weak sentences.

causes.title: A plot pitch with no stakes
causes.text: QueryTracker ranks an uninteresting plot description second. Matesic also lists an underwhelming plot blurb as a reason. The usual pattern is a list of events. The letter says what happens, but not what the character wants, what blocks them, or what they lose if they fail. Agents need all three near the top to judge whether they want to read more.

causes.title: Wrong genre, age category, or agent
causes.text: A letter can be fine and still land on the wrong desk. QueryTracker ranks wrong genre or age category third. Matesic lists lack of interest in the genre or in what the agent currently wants as a reason. A strong middle grade fantasy sent to an agent who handles only adult thrillers is a mismatch, even if the writing is good.

causes.title: A dull opening and weak sample pages
causes.text: QueryTracker ranks a boring opening sixth. Matesic says uninteresting sample pages are the most common reason she sees, though she gives no numbers. An agent who likes the letter can still pass if the first pages slow down. The letter promises a book, and the pages must deliver that promise.

causes.title: Tone, length, and guideline misses
causes.text: QueryTracker places unprofessional tone or attitude fourth, problematic length fifth, and incorrect formatting or missing information last. These are easy to fix and easy to miss. A letter that ignores an agent's posted rules can be dropped before anyone reads the pitch. Query Shark says it discards queries that do not follow its posted directions.

fixes.title: Rewrite the pitch around want, obstacle, and cost
fixes.text: Write one sentence for each part. The first says what the main character wants. The second says what stands in the way. The third says what they lose if they fail. Build the pitch in that order and cut any sentence that does not move one of the three. Then test it on someone who has not read the book.

fixes.title: Cut the letter to one page or less
fixes.text: QueryTracker advises one page or less, about 300 to 400 words. In Word, open Tools > Word Count to see the total. In Pages, ask Lazur to circle where the count appears on screen. Trim credits and comps first, since they are optional.

fixes.title: Put the layout in the right order
fixes.text: Place the title and genre at the top, then the rounded word count, then the pitch. Add credits or comps only if they help the case. Pages starts every document from a template you can replace, so begin with a plain one and remove the decorative parts.

fixes.title: Fix the first page before you send
fixes.text: Read your first page as a stranger would. Mark every line where you want to skim, and rewrite those lines first. Ask whether the page answers the question the pitch raised. Sample pages are a common reason for a pass, so this fix matters as much as the letter.

fixes.title: Match each agent to your book
fixes.text: Open each agent's own page or website. Check the genre, the age category, and what the agent says they want now. Skip agents whose list does not fit. A short list you can defend beats a long list of mismatches, and it costs you less waiting.

fixes.title: Follow every posted rule
fixes.text: Copy each agent's guidelines into one note. Check the letter against them line by line before you paste it into an email. Send exactly what the agent asks for and nothing extra. Query Shark, a critique blog, discards queries that ignore its posted directions, so treat every agent's page the same way.

fixes.title: Get a read from a writing group
fixes.text: A critique group can name what confuses a reader in the pitch. Ask for one specific answer, such as whether the stakes are clear, not a general opinion. Group quality varies, so compare notes from more than one reader before you rewrite again.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Read the letter cold
plan.text: Read the letter once, out loud, as a stranger would. Mark each sentence that feels like setup. Write one line each for want, obstacle, and cost.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Rewrite the pitch
plan.text: Rebuild the pitch in the three-part order. Read it out loud, one paragraph at a time, and cut anything that drifts from the main character's problem.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Check length and layout
plan.text: Aim for one page or less and about 300 to 400 words. Confirm the title, the genre, and the rounded word count sit at the top.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Match the agents
plan.text: Open each agent's own page. Check the genre, the age category, and what they want now. Keep only the agents whose list fits your book.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Send a small batch
plan.text: Send to a small batch and log each send with the version, the date, and the agent. Do not reply to form rejections. Wait for the batch to answer before you change anything.
